title: Yesterday’s Man
author: Nathan Pinkoski
content:
![Yesterday’s
Man](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/11/IMG_5293.jpg)

> _In the Realm of the Last Man: A Memoir_  
>  By Francis Fukuyama  
> FSG, 304 pages, $29

The publishing industry is experiencing a surge in memoirs, and the Boomers
are to blame. They want to reflect on their lives and describe the vanished
world of their youth before they themselves vanish from the earth. It's [_a
surge_](https://www.the-independent.com/arts-entertainment/books/memoir-books-
misery-faulks-dyer-b2842636.html?ref=compactmag.com) in supply, not a surge in
demand. Readers are skeptical the Boomers have something to say. But if the
memoir of any member of that generation deserves a hearing, it is Francis
Fukuyama's.

Born in 1952 to a family of first- and second-generation Japanese immigrants,
Fukuyama vaulted to fame with his 1989 essay "[_The End of
History?_](https://www.google.com/search?q=summer+1989+%E2%80%9CThe+End+of+History%E2%80%9D+essay&oq=summer+1989+%E2%80%9CThe+End+of+History%E2%80%9D+essay&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUyBggAEEUYOTIHCAEQIRigATIHCAIQIRigATIHCAMQIRigATIHCAQQIRigAdIBBzI2N2owajeoAgCwAgA&sourceid=chrome&source=chrome.ob&ie=UTF-8),"
becoming one of the world's most celebrated public intellectuals. His memoir,
_In the Realm of the Last Man_ , is marketed as a personal and intellectual
autobiography that also provides an apologia for his most famous thesis. The
book checks off several boxes of the memoir genre. Fukuyama describes his
family origins, childhood, education, and his first professional postings with
the RAND Corporation, the CIA, and the State Department prior to publishing
his famous essay. He reflects on his personal hobbies (he is an amateur
computer coder and carpenter). He reminisces about his intellectual
influences: Leo Strauss and his student Allan Bloom, the social scientist
Seymour Martin Lipset, and the political scientist Samuel Huntington. Modest
and laconic about his political connections, Fukuyama regales readers with
amusing anecdotes of an audience with Muammar Gaddafi and a more personal
friendship with a senior official in the Chinese government. He also explains
why, [_like most of his
generation_](https://academic.oup.com/poq/article/85/4/1009/6458238?ref=compactmag.com),
he has become less conservative over time.

> "The book isn't really a memoir."

Yet the book isn't really a memoir. A few pages in, as Fukuyama recounts his
family's history in America, he abruptly veers off from talking about
relatives interned during the Second World War to declare that "in 2025, the
US returned to mistreating people--this time, those suspected of being
undocumented migrants." Most of the book is like that. Every few pages,
Fukuyama connects an old story, teacher, or lesson learned to some deplorable
recent action by Donald Trump or his allies. The book begins with Trump's
second inauguration, casting him as a world-historical figure dismantling the
postwar liberal order. It ends by invoking the challenge Christian
nationalists and the "strong gods" pose to liberalism. At the heart of _In the
Realm of the Last Man_ is Fukuyama's struggle to explain the success of
emerging political movements, particularly Trump's, which repudiate the
consensus he helped define in his youth. What he doesn't acknowledge is that
many of his intellectual shifts mirror those of the movements he despises.
